```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4)
library(cyclind)
# Numbers quoted in the text are computed from these files.
calib <- function(file) {
  utils::read.csv(system.file("calibration", file, package = "cyclind"),
                  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}
pct <- function(x, digits = 0) {
  paste(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = digits), "percent")
}
pct_range <- function(x, digits = 0) {
  paste(formatC(100 * min(x), format = "f", digits = digits), "to",
        pct(max(x), digits))
}
f2 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
f3 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3)
pp <- function(x) formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = 1)
```

A composite leading indicator (CLI) combines series whose cycles turn before
the business cycle. `cyclind` builds on the OECD system of composite
leading indicators (Gyomai and Guidetti 2012; Gyomai, Ahmad and Astolfi
2017), from the choice of candidates to a tested composite, and adds the
statistical checks recommended in the literature on leading indicators
(Marcellino 2006). Where its defaults depart from the OECD documents, the
section "The OECD method and the defaults" says so and gives the evidence.

All examples use simulated data from `simulate_cycles()`, in which the
truth is known, and the calibration results shipped in
`inst/calibration/`. `vignette("oecd-indonesia")` applies the OECD method
to public OECD data for Indonesia.

## 1. Candidates and specification

Every workflow starts with a reference series and candidate series at the
same frequency. Here we simulate thirty years of monthly data: two series
lead by six and three months, one is coincident, one lags, one is
counter-cyclical and two are noise.

```{r data}
sim <- simulate_cycles(seed = 2026)
attr(sim, "truth")
```

The OECD asks for an economic rationale for every component; statistics
do not replace it. `cyclind` records it and warns when it is missing.

```{r candidates}
meta <- data.frame(
  name = colnames(sim)[-1],
  rationale = c("early_stage", "rapid_response", "rapid_response",
                "rapid_response", "expectations", "prime_mover",
                "prime_mover")
)
cand <- cli_candidates(sim, reference = "reference", meta = meta)
cand
```

All methodological choices live in one specification object:

```{r spec}
spec <- cli_spec(freq = 12)
spec
```

## 2. The whole workflow in one call

```{r build}
res <- cli_build(cand, spec)
res
```

`cli_build()` extracts the cycles, dates the turning points, classifies
every candidate, aggregates the leading ones and tests the composite. The
classification table shows why each series was kept or rejected:

```{r assessment}
assessment(res)
```

The counter-cyclical series was inverted before it was assessed. Its
direction was read from the cross-correlation within a quarter of the
average reference cycle; a longer window would let the opposite phase of
a regular cycle decide. Where the direction is known from the economic
rationale, declare it in a `sign` column of `meta` (1 or -1): leads beyond
a quarter of the cycle cannot be told apart from inversion by the data.
The audit log records each iteration of the selection loop:

```{r audit}
audit_log(res)[, c("iteration", "action", "components", "ccf_lag",
                   "passed")]
```

```{r plot, fig.alt = "Composite and reference cycles, contractions shaded"}
plot(res)
```

## 3. Step by step

Every step is also available on its own, so a workflow can stop anywhere,
for example after the classification.

```{r steps}
cyc <- cli_cycles(cand, spec)
cyc$lead_6
tp <- cli_turning_points(cyc, spec)
head(as.data.frame(tp$reference))
cli <- cli_composite(cyc, c("lead_6", "lead_3"), spec, cyc$reference)
cli_validate(cli, cyc$reference, spec)
```

Filters (the double Hodrick-Prescott filter of Hodrick and Prescott 1997
by default, or the band-pass filter of Christiano and Fitzgerald 2003),
turning-point rules (Bry and Boschan 1971; Harding and Pagan 2002) and
aggregation methods are interchangeable objects:

```{r alternatives}
alt <- update(spec, filter = cf_filter(), aggregator = dynamic_factor())
components(cli_build(cand, alt))
```

### Matching turning points

A reference turning point is paired with a candidate turning point of the
same type inside `lead_window` (`c(12, 24)` by default: up to 24 months
lead and 12 months lag). When several candidate turning points fall in
the window, `matching = "nearest"` (the default) takes the one closest in
time and `matching = "maximum"` the most pronounced one:

```{r matching}
res_max <- cli_build(cand, update(spec, matching = "maximum"))
med <- function(r) {
  a <- as.data.frame(assessment(r))
  stats::setNames(a$median_lead, a$name)
}
rbind(nearest = med(res), maximum = med(res_max))
```

```{r matching-numbers, include = FALSE}
d_match <- med(res_max) - med(res)
n_match <- sum(d_match != 0, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Here the rule changes the median lead of `r n_match` of the
`r length(d_match)` candidates; the leading components are the same
(`r paste(components(res_max), collapse = ", ")`).

### Outliers, twins and agreement

Every outlier treatment reports what it found. The simulated series have
no outliers, so we add a spike of 30 percent to one month of `lead_3`;
`outlier_report()` lists, series by series, the outliers replaced and
(in brackets in the column `periods`) those detected but kept:

```{r outliers}
sim_o <- sim
k <- which(abs(stats::time(sim) - (2010 + 5 / 12)) < 1e-6)
sim_o[k, "lead_3"] <- sim_o[k, "lead_3"] * 1.3
cyc_o <- cli_cycles(cli_candidates(sim_o, "reference", meta = meta), spec)
rep_o <- outlier_report(cyc_o)
rep_o[rep_o$name %in% c("reference", "lead_3"),
      c("name", "n_removed", "periods", "types")]
```

A share of replaced outliers above `max_share` (5 percent by default)
gives a warning. Two candidates that carry the same information, such as
a series and a copy of it in other units, would double its weight in the
composite. Before the selection loop, candidates whose cycles correlate
at least `twin_threshold` (0.99 by default) in absolute value are reduced
to the one with the higher cross-correlation with the reference, with a
warning and a line in the audit log. Here `twin` is `lead_6` in other
units with a small disturbance:

```{r twins}
wiggle <- 1 + 0.002 * sin(seq_len(nrow(sim)))
sim_t <- cbind(sim, twin = 2 * sim[, "lead_6"] * wiggle)
colnames(sim_t) <- c(colnames(sim), "twin")
meta_t <- rbind(meta, data.frame(name = "twin", rationale = "early_stage"))
res_t <- cli_build(cli_candidates(sim_t, "reference", meta = meta_t), spec)
audit_log(res_t)[1, c("iteration", "action")]
```

`cycle_agreement()` compares a cycle with the reference by the Pearson
and Spearman correlations and the root mean squared error of the
normalised cycles, outside excluded periods such as a crisis. With
`reps > 0` it adds paired moving-block bootstrap intervals; the draws
start from an explicit `seed` and leave the random numbers of the session
untouched. Here the composite is compared with the reference without
2008 and the first half of 2009:

```{r agreement}
cycle_agreement(composite(res), cyc$reference, exclude = c(2008, 2009.5),
                reps = 199, seed = 1)
```

The correlation at lag 0 understates the agreement of a leading
composite, whose cycle is shifted by its lead.

## 4. Growth cycles, growth rate cycles and classical cycles

The OECD presents a CLI in three forms, each read against its own kind of
cycle (Gyomai and Guidetti 2012, pp. 9–11):

* the **growth cycle**: the deviation of the level from its long-term
  trend, an output-gap reading. The OECD dates its turning points on this
  form. A peak marks output starting to fall back towards its trend.
* the **classical cycle** (business cycle) of the level itself. The OECD
  reaches it by restoring the trend: the trend-restored CLI is the
  amplitude-adjusted CLI times the trend of the reference series. Its
  peaks come later and its troughs earlier than those of the growth
  cycle.
* the **growth rate cycle**: the 12-month rate of change of the
  trend-restored CLI, compared with the growth rate of GDP. A peak marks
  growth starting to slow down; it usually marks an inflection point of
  the growth cycle, and its lead is not stable (Gyomai and Guidetti
  2012, p. 12).

In cyclind the kind of cycle is set by the `form` of the specification.
`level_form()`, the default, gives the growth cycle. It is paired with
`hp_double_filter()`, the double Hodrick-Prescott filter of the OECD: a
first filter removes the trend (cycles longer than 120 months, or 40
quarters) and a second one smooths away movements shorter than 12 months
(4 quarters). `growth_form()` gives the growth rate cycle. A logged
series becomes its growth rate over `lag` periods (one year by default),

$$g_t = 100 \left(\frac{Y_t}{Y_{t-k}} - 1\right),$$

the rate as statistical offices publish it (`rate = "log"` gives the log
rate $100 (\log Y_t - \log Y_{t-k})$). A series in levels, or a candidate
whose `unit` in the metadata is `"percent"` (an interest rate, a balance
of opinion), is differenced in its own units, $Y_t - Y_{t-k}$. Rates are
computed after seasonal adjustment and the treatment of outliers. Growth
rates have little trend, so `growth_form()` is paired with
`hp_smoother()`, which only smooths.

```{r forms}
spec_g <- cli_spec(freq = 12, form = growth_form())
spec_g@filter
cyc_g <- cli_cycles(cand, spec_g)
tail(cyc_g$reference@steps, 3)
tp_g <- cli_turning_points(cyc_g, spec_g)
c(growth_cycle = nrow(as.data.frame(tp$reference)),
  growth_rate_cycle = nrow(as.data.frame(tp_g$reference)))
```

The growth rate cycle of the simulated reference has
`r nrow(as.data.frame(tp_g$reference))` turning points against
`r nrow(as.data.frame(tp$reference))` in its growth cycle:

```{r forms-plot, fig.height = 5}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   Growth cycle and growth rate cycle of the simulated reference series
#|   with their turning points
show_cycle <- function(cs, tps, main) {
  plot(cs@normalised, ylab = "Normalised", xlab = NULL, main = main)
  abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
  d <- as.data.frame(tps)
  points(d$time, d$value, pch = ifelse(d$type == "peak", 25, 24),
         bg = "grey50")
}
op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 1), mar = c(2, 4, 2, 1))
show_cycle(cyc$reference, tp$reference, "Growth cycle (level_form())")
legend("topleft", c("peak", "trough"), pch = c(25, 24), pt.bg = "grey50",
       horiz = TRUE, bty = "n")
show_cycle(cyc_g$reference, tp_g$reference,
           "Growth rate cycle (growth_form())")
par(op)
```

The classical cycle is not a form of the specification: cyclind
classifies candidates on growth cycles or growth rate cycles, and
`cli_presentation()` turns a growth-cycle composite into the
trend-restored CLI and its 12-month rate of change, as the OECD does:

```{r presentation}
pres <- cli_presentation(res)
tail(pres[, c("time", "amplitude_adjusted", "trend_restored",
              "rate_of_change", "reference")], 3)
```

The thresholds of the classifiers were calibrated on growth cycles, so the
growth rate form is experimental. `data-raw/calibrate_forms.R` measures
the default rules on both forms:

```{r forms-calibration}
fm <- calib("forms.csv")
fm[, c("form", "freq", "noise_sd", "correct.leading", "false_leading",
       "overall")]
```

```{r forms-numbers, include = FALSE}
fm_g <- fm[fm$form == "growth", ]
fm_l <- fm[fm$form == "level", ]
```

On these simulations the rules find leaders in growth rate cycles about as
often as in growth cycles and label at most
`r pct(max(fm_g$false_leading), 1)` of the others leading, but the overall
share of correct classes is lower with strong noise
(`r f3(min(fm_g$overall))` against `r f3(min(fm_l$overall))`).

## 5. How the classification rules were calibrated

The thresholds were not guessed. The script `data-raw/calibrate_collect.R`
simulates 100 samples for each frequency and three noise levels, classifies
every candidate and compares the class with the truth.

```{r calibration}
acc <- calib("accuracy.csv")
acc[, c("freq", "noise_sd", "correct.leading", "correct.rejected",
        "false_leading", "overall")]
```

```{r calibration-numbers, include = FALSE}
st <- calib("assessment-stats.csv")
noise <- st[st$truth == "rejected", ]
lead <- st[st$truth == "leading", ]
no_granger <- function(d) mean(d$reasons %in% c("", "granger"))
with_granger <- function(d) mean(d$reasons == "")
cell <- interaction(noise$freq, noise$noise_sd)
other_class <- tapply(noise$class %in% c("coincident", "lagging"), cell,
                      mean)
nonlead <- st[st$truth != "leading", ]
n_cell <- max(table(interaction(nonlead$freq, nonlead$noise_sd)))
p_max <- max(acc$false_leading)
ts_conc <- calib("test-size.csv")
ts_conc <- ts_conc[ts_conc$study == "concordance" &
                     ts_conc$series == "independent", ]
nw <- ts_conc$value[grepl("^reject_nw", ts_conc$statistic)]
fb <- ts_conc$value[grepl("^reject_fixedb_(median|fixed)$",
                          ts_conc$statistic)]
```

Two lessons shaped the defaults:

* the median lead at turning points shrinks towards zero as noise grows,
  whereas the lead of the cross-correlation peak stays unbiased, so the
  cross-correlation lead is the primary lead measure;
* without the Granger causality test of Toda and Yamamoto (1995), the
  other criteria label
  `r pct(no_granger(noise), 1)` of the pure-noise series leading; with it,
  `r pct(with_granger(noise), 2)`, while the share of true leaders found
  falls only from `r pct(no_granger(lead), 1)` to
  `r pct(with_granger(lead), 1)` (`inst/calibration/assessment-stats.csv`).

With low or moderate noise most candidates are classified correctly, and
non-leading series are almost never labelled leading. With quarterly data
and strong noise the power to detect leaders falls: thirty years give only
120 observations. Pure-noise series are then also called coincident or
lagging more often (up to `r pct(max(other_class))`), which does no harm
to the composite. The rules were tuned and then evaluated on the same
simulation design (cycles of four years, thirty years of data), so these
rates are optimistic for other designs. With 100 samples per cell and
`r n_cell` non-leading series, the largest rate of false leaders,
`r pct(p_max, 1)`, has a Monte Carlo standard error of about
`r f2(100 * sqrt(p_max * (1 - p_max) / n_cell))` percentage points.

The tests behind the criteria allow for the persistence of cycles. Phases
last years, so the usual Newey-West variance made the concordance test
reject independent cycles `r pct_range(nw)` of the time at the 5 percent
level; with the fixed-b variance of Kiefer and Vogelsang (2005) it rejects
`r pct_range(fb)` (`inst/calibration/test-size.csv`, which also records
the size of the Pesaran-Timmermann test and of the prediction criteria).

## 6. Is the in-sample lead real?

Components are chosen because they led in the sample, so the in-sample
lead overstates the lead to expect later. `cli_selection_bias()` chooses
the components with data up to a cut-off date and measures the lead of
that composite only at later turning points.

```{r bias}
sb <- cli_selection_bias(cand, spec, cutoffs = c(2014, 2017))
sb[, c("cutoff", "components", "median_lead_in", "median_lead_out",
       "n_tp_out", "lead_gap")]
```

In this simulation the leaders are genuine, so the lead after each cut-off
is at least as long as before it (`lead_gap` of `r paste(sb$lead_gap, collapse =
" and ")` months). With real data a large positive `lead_gap` means the
in-sample lead is mostly a selection effect. Set `oos_cutoffs` in the
specification to run this check inside `cli_build()`.

## 7. Is the composite good enough?

`cli_quality()` turns the validation into a scorecard with a verdict. It
checks three groups of criteria:

* **turning points**: the composite meets every leading criterion used to
  classify candidates;
* **prediction**: out-of-sample probabilities of contraction, each from a
  logit fitted to earlier periods only, have an area under the ROC curve of
  at least 0.7 and a quadratic probability score below that of the naive
  forecast from the same past data, and the Pesaran and Timmermann (2009)
  test finds
  that the composite's direction predicts the later direction of the
  reference. The horizon is fixed in advance (the lower end of
  `target_lead`, 6 months by default), not taken from the composite;
* **out of sample**: after the cut-off dates the composite still leads, and
  the in-sample lead does not exceed the later lead by more than `min_lead`.

The verdict is *good* when all three groups pass, *acceptable* when the
first two groups pass but the out-of-sample check was not run, and *weak*
otherwise.

```{r quality}
res_oos <- cli_build(cand, update(spec, oos_cutoffs = c(2014, 2017)))
cli_quality(res_oos)
```

## 8. Mixed frequencies and variable types

`cyclind` works at one frequency, but the data rarely arrive that way: GDP
is quarterly, credit is a monthly stock, exchange rates are daily, some
sales are weekly. `cli_align()` brings them to one frequency with the rule
set by the type of each series (`series_types`): flows are summed, stocks
are taken at the end of the period, averages are averaged. Weekly data are
spread over their days before they are summed into months, so that months
of five weeks do not look larger than months of four. A quarterly
reference series is disaggregated to months with the Denton-Cholette
method (Denton 1971) or the Chow-Lin method (Chow and Lin 1971) with a
monthly indicator that is not a candidate; quarterly candidates are
interpolated at the month the OECD uses (central month, or last month for
stocks; Gyomai and Guidetti 2012, p. 6).

```{r align}
gdp_q <- aggregate(sim[, "reference"], nfrequency = 4, FUN = sum)
weeks <- seq(as.Date("1995-01-02"), as.Date("2024-12-23"), by = "week")
set.seed(1)
sales <- data.frame(date = weeks,
                    value = 700 * exp(cumsum(rnorm(length(weeks), 0,
                                                   0.01))))
x <- cli_align(list(gdp = gdp_q, sim[, -1], sales = sales),
               type = c(gdp = "flow", sales = "flow"), reference = "gdp")
attr(x, "alignment")[c(1, 9), ]
cand_mf <- cli_candidates(x, reference = "gdp",
                          meta = data.frame(name = colnames(x)[-1],
                                            rationale = "early_stage"))
res_mf <- cli_build(cand_mf)
leaders(res_mf)
```

When the reference series was disaggregated, the quality scorecard adds a
line saying that its turning-point dates, and so the lead, are uncertain by
about one month: the monthly path inside each quarter is an estimate.

Data published as one file per indicator, at different frequencies, are
read with `read_cli_series()`: each file has a date column (`2001-01-15`,
`15/01/2001`, `2001-01`, `2001Q1`, `2001S1` or `2001`) and one or more
value columns, and the result goes straight into `cli_align()`.

The source frequency of every series (`series_frequencies`) is detected
from its dates and recorded with the candidates (`cand_mf@meta$frequency`);
`cli_align(frequency = )` checks a declared frequency against the data. A
semiannual or annual series can only be the reference: it is disaggregated
like a quarterly one; with Denton-Cholette (the default) or Chow-Lin every
year (or half-year) is kept exactly, and the scorecard notes that its
turning-point dates are uncertain by about half a source period. A
candidate needs at least quarterly data, since one value a year cannot show
a lead of a few months.

```{r align-annual}
gdp_a <- aggregate(sim[, "reference"], nfrequency = 1, FUN = sum)
x_a <- cli_align(list(gdp = gdp_a, sim[, -1]), type = c(gdp = "flow"),
                 reference = "gdp", frequency = c(gdp = "annual"))
attr(x_a, "alignment")[1, ]
all.equal(as.numeric(aggregate(x_a[, "gdp"], nfrequency = 1, FUN = sum)),
          as.numeric(gdp_a))
```

Moving holidays, such as the Eid al-Fitr holiday (Idulfitri) in
Indonesia, shift through the calendar, so fixed seasonal factors miss
them. Holiday effects are optional (by default `holidays = list()`) and
apply only with `seasonal_adjust = TRUE`. `holiday_effect()` turns the
dates of any moving holiday (Easter, Chinese New Year, Diwali, ...) into
regressors for X-13ARIMA-SEATS (package **seasonal**);
`idulfitri_dates()` is a helper for Idulfitri:

```{r holidays, eval = FALSE}
eid <- holiday_effect(idulfitri_dates(1990, 2030), name = "idulfitri")
spec_sa <- cli_spec(seasonal_adjust = TRUE, holidays = eid)
```

X-13 forecasts three years past the end of the data, and the holiday
regressors must cover those years too: for data ending in 2027 the dates
above, up to 2030, are just enough. With dates that stop earlier the
series are adjusted with X-11 without forecasts and `cli_cycles()` warns
once (`cyclind_warning_holiday_horizon`).

Dates and effects are country-specific. `idulfitri_dates()` gives the
arithmetic (tabular) Islamic calendar; the official date of 1 Syawal is
set by each country (in Indonesia by the Ministry of Religious Affairs
after the *sidang isbat*, elsewhere by other authorities, by moon
sighting or by calculation) and can differ from it, and between countries,
by a day or two. The default windows, two weeks before the holiday and
the week of collective leave that starts on it, describe Indonesia
(*mudik* and *cuti bersama*). For another country give its official dates
and its own `windows`, e.g.
`holiday_effect(official_dates, name = "eid", windows = list(before =
c(-7, -1), after = c(0, 2)))`.

## 9. The OECD method and the defaults

`oecd_spec()` follows the OECD documents (Gyomai and Guidetti 2012,
"GG12"; Gyomai, Ahmad and Astolfi 2017, "GAA17") where they state a rule.
The table gives the source of each step and marks the choices of cyclind
where the documents give no formula:

| Step | OECD rule (source) | `oecd_spec()` | `cli_spec()` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Outliers | TRAMO; additive outliers removed, level shifts on expert judgement, transitory changes not mentioned (GAA17 p. 283) | `tramo_outliers()`, `outlier_types = "AO"` (cyclind: TC kept) | robust z-score |
| Target cycle | growth cycle; growth rate and classical CLIs are presentations (GAA17 pp. 276--277) | `level_form()` | same |
| Log or levels | TRAMO test (GAA17 p. 284) | `transform = "test"` | `"auto"` |
| End of series | 2--6 months of TRAMO forecasts (GAA17 p. 284) | 2 months | 12 months, AR |
| Cycle | double HP, 12--120 months (GG12 pp. 7, 15) | same | same |
| Normalisation | mean, mean absolute deviation (GG12 p. 7) | same | same |
| Turning points | Bry-Boschan, phase 9, cycle 24 months (GAA17 p. 285) | `oecd_dater()` | `bry_boschan()`, 5/15 |
| Matching window | 24 months lead, 9 lag (GAA17 p. 285) | `c(9, 24)` | `c(12, 24)` |
| Evaluation | lead, conformity, missing or extra cycles, no thresholds (GG12 p. 8) | 40 percent, fixed-b test, positive peak (cyclind) | calibrated thresholds |
| Classification | median lead, coincident within 2 months, no minimum of turning points (GG12 p. 9) | `oecd_classifier()`, `min_matched = 3` (cyclind) | `cyclind_classifier()` |
| Lag-shifting | not used in practice (GAA17 p. 287) | off | off |
| Aggregation | chained mean of ratios, 60 percent rule (GAA17 p. 286, note 8) | chained mean log ratio (cyclind) | `equal_weight()` |
| Amplitude | rescaled to the reference, measure not given (GAA17 p. 288) | standard deviation (cyclind) | mean absolute deviation |
| Trend restored | not computed while GDP is missing (OECD 2024, question 6) | same | same |

For quarterly data `oecd_spec()` uses phases of 3 and cycles of 8
quarters and a matching window of 3 quarters lag and 8 lead; these are
cyclind's translation of the monthly rules. The TRAMO steps run through
RJDemetra or, without Java, the regARIMA part of X-13. Which turning point
of a phase that is too short the OECD drops is not documented; both
daters keep the most extreme ones (`phase_rule = "symmetric"`, see
`?Dater`), so that dating the reversed series gives the same turning
points. The original 5/15-month rule, which the OECD used before 2008
(GG12, annex B), is `oecd_spec(dater = bry_boschan())`. Where the OECD
documents name a criterion without a threshold or a formula, the choice
is cyclind's: the thresholds of the conformity criteria (at most 40
percent missed or extra turning points, concordance significant at 5
percent with the fixed-b test, a positive cross-correlation peak), the
minimum of three matched turning points (`min_matched = 3`), the
aggregation by mean log ratios with the inversion of counter-cyclical
components, and the amplitude measure.

The choices of cyclind, in one list (each can be changed in
`oecd_spec()` or `oecd_classifier()`):

* `outlier_types = "AO"`: GAA17 (p. 283) filters additive outliers and
  removes level shifts only on expert judgement; it does not mention
  transitory changes, which cyclind keeps. When an additive outlier and a
  transitory change are found on the same date, their regressors are
  nearly collinear (correlation 0.96 for quarterly X-13), and cyclind
  takes the additive outlier as the whole deviation at that date and the
  transitory change as the decay after it, with a warning
  (`cyclind_warning_outlier_collinear`; `?OutlierTreatment`).
* `min_matched = 3`, the 40 percent limits of missed and extra turning
  points and the fixed-b test of concordance (`?oecd_classifier`).
* aggregation by mean log ratios with reciprocal inversion
  (`oecd_aggregate()`), and the standard deviation as amplitude measure.
* quarterly mode: phases of 3 and cycles of 8 quarters, a matching window
  of 3 and 8 quarters.
* the transformation decided by cyclind (`transform`) is also passed to
  the X-13 seasonal adjustment, and a series that X-13 cannot adjust is
  kept unadjusted when the QS test finds no seasonality, adjusted again
  without holiday regressors, or left out with its reason
  (`cyclind_warning_seasonal_failed`, `excluded_series()`).

```{r oecd, eval = FALSE}
res_oecd <- cli_build(cand, oecd_spec())
outlier_report(res_oecd)
tail(cli_presentation(res_oecd))
```

### Evidence from simulations

The package defaults differ where the simulations in
`data-raw/compare_oecd.R` showed a gain. Classified with the OECD rule,
the calibration candidates give these rates:

```{r oecd-classification}
cmp <- calib("oecd-classification.csv")
cmp[cmp$rule != "OECD (min 1 matched)", ]
```

```{r oecd-numbers, include = FALSE}
by_rule <- function(rule) cmp[cmp$rule == rule, ]
med_only <- by_rule("OECD (median lead only)")
oecd3 <- by_rule("OECD (min 3 matched)")
own <- by_rule("cyclind")
key <- function(d) paste(d$freq, d$noise_sd)
oecd3 <- oecd3[match(key(med_only), key(oecd3)), ]
own <- own[match(key(med_only), key(own)), ]
loss <- med_only$leading_found - oecd3$leading_found
gain <- oecd3$leading_found - own$leading_found
noisy <- med_only$noise_sd == max(med_only$noise_sd)
```

The median lead alone (`oecd_classifier(conformity = FALSE)`) labels
`r pct_range(med_only$false_leading)` of the non-leading candidates
leading, and up to `r pct(max(med_only$noise_called_leading))` of the
pure-noise series. With the conformity criteria, the default, the OECD
rule labels `r pct_range(oecd3$false_leading, 1)` of them leading; it finds
at most `r pp(max(loss[!noisy]))` percentage points fewer true leaders
than the median lead alone with low or moderate noise, and
`r pp(min(loss[noisy]))` to `r pp(max(loss[noisy]))` fewer with strong
noise. The default rule of the package labels at most
`r pct(max(own$false_leading), 1)` of the others leading, but finds up to
`r pp(max(gain))` percentage points fewer leaders than the OECD rule in
noisy data.

```{r oecd-aggregation}
agg <- calib("oecd-aggregation.csv")
agg
```

```{r aggregation-numbers, include = FALSE}
re <- agg[!agg$lag_shift, ]
re_err <- function(a) re$ragged_edge_error[re$aggregation == a]
shift_loss <- agg$ccf_lag[!agg$lag_shift] - agg$ccf_lag[agg$lag_shift]
```

The plain mean (`level`), the mean chained at the ragged edge (`chain`, the
default) and the full OECD chain (`oecd`) give nearly the same composite in
sample, but when the longest-lead component misses its last two values
both chained forms stay closer to the full-information composite (an
error of `r f3(min(re_err("chain")))` to `r f3(max(re_err("chain")))`
against `r f3(min(re_err("level")))` to `r f3(max(re_err("level")))` for
the plain mean). Lag-shifting makes the leads more consistent and the
composite misses fewer turning points, but it shortens the
cross-correlation lead of the composite by `r f2(min(shift_loss))` to
`r f2(max(shift_loss))` months, towards the shortest lead of the
components; it is therefore off by default, as in OECD practice.

Two OECD ideas are defaults because of a real-time study
(`data-raw/realtime_defaults.R`): chaining at the ragged edge
(`equal_weight()`, chained only after the last date at which all
components are observed, so that a component that starts late changes
nothing) and extending each series with one year of forecasts before the
filter (`ar_extension()`, an autoregression of the changes instead of
TRAMO, which needs no other software). The table compares the last value
of pseudo real-time composites with the full-sample composite:

```{r realtime-defaults}
rt <- calib("realtime-defaults.csv")
rt
```

```{r realtime-numbers, include = FALSE}
rt_v <- function(v, col) rt[rt$variant == v, col]
dir_gain <- rt_v("chain only", "direction_right") -
  rt_v("neither", "direction_right")
rev_cut <- rt_v("neither", "revision") - rt_v("AR only", "revision")
```

Chaining makes the direction of the last change right more often (by
`r pp(min(dir_gain))` to `r pp(max(dir_gain))` percentage points); the
extension makes the revision of the
last value smaller (by `r f3(min(rev_cut))` to `r f3(max(rev_cut))`); the
defaults have both. The classification is hardly affected (section 5 shows
the thresholds recalibrated with the extension), so the thresholds were
kept. To use neither:

```{r old-defaults, eval = FALSE}
cli_spec(aggregator = equal_weight(ragged_edge = "level"),
         extension = no_extension())
```

The length of the extension differs between programs. cyclind appends one
year of AR forecasts of the changes (12 months or 4 quarters;
`ar_extension(h = )` changes it); the OECD appends 2 to 6 months of TRAMO
forecasts (GAA17 p. 284; `oecd_spec()` uses 2); the Python package CIF
(Vraná 2020), which implements the OECD method, appends six months of
ARIMA forecasts by default. A longer extension moves more of the
end-point revision of the two-sided filter into the forecast error, so
the end of the cycle leans more on the model. Switching the outliers of
`oecd_spec()` off (`update(spec, outlier_threshold = Inf)`) keeps its
forecasts through `regarima_extension()`, so the two options stay
separate.

`oecd_spec()` replaces additive outliers only (`outlier_types = "AO"`,
GAA17 p. 283); transitory changes and level shifts are reported by
`outlier_report()` but kept. TRAMO-type outliers and the robust default
classify the candidates about equally well when spikes and a level shift
are injected:

```{r oecd-outliers}
calib("oecd-outliers.csv")
```

### Replication: the OECD CLI of Indonesia

The OECD publishes, through its SDMX interface, the CLI of Indonesia, its
reference series (monthly GDP) and its seven components (consumer
confidence, the rupiah exchange rate, production of non-metallic products,
producer prices, share prices, the short-term interest rate and tourism
activity). The components are published only as normalised cycles, and
for four of them the OECD also publishes the original series.
`data-raw/oecd_idn_fetch.R` saves a snapshot; `data-raw/oecd_idn_validate.R`
runs two experiments. In the first, the OECD cycles go into cyclind as they
are; in the second, the original series go through
`oecd_spec(engine = "tramo")`. The stored numbers were made with TRAMO
(RJDemetra 0.2.8); with the X-13 engine, which `engine = "auto"` takes when
RJDemetra is missing, the second experiment gives other numbers (the GDP
cycle correlates 0.912 instead of 0.992 with the OECD reference cycle), so
the script stops without RJDemetra.

```{r oecd-idn-composite}
idn <- calib("oecd-idn-composite.csv")
idn[, c("composite", "corr_lag0", "aa_gap", "matched", "ref_tp",
        "ref_ccf_lag")]
```

```{r idn-numbers, include = FALSE}
row <- function(prefix) idn[startsWith(idn$composite, prefix), ]
gaps <- calib("oecd-idn-gaps.csv")
gap <- function(pattern) {
  gaps$value[grepl(pattern, gaps$variant, fixed = TRUE)]
}
comp <- calib("oecd-idn-components.csv")
lab <- c(LOCOCI = "consumer confidence", LOCOEX = "the exchange rate",
         LOCOPM = "production of non-metallic products",
         LOCOPP = "producer prices", LOCOSP = "share prices",
         LOCOST = "the interest rate", LOCOTA = "tourism activity")
words <- function(x) {
  x <- unname(lab[x])
  if (length(x) < 2) return(x)
  paste(paste(x[-length(x)], collapse = ", "), "and", x[length(x)])
}
cmp_c <- comp[comp$component != "RS", ]
inv_oecd <- cmp_c$component[cmp_c$oecd_sign == "inverted"]
inv_own <- cmp_c$component[cmp_c$cyclind_sign == "inverted"]
missed_sign <- setdiff(inv_oecd, inv_own)
pp_r <- cmp_c$A_ccf_r[cmp_c$component == "LOCOPP"]
b_corr <- comp$B_corr_with_oecd_cycle[!is.na(comp$B_corr_with_oecd_cycle)]
rs <- comp[comp$component == "RS", ]
bench <- row("OECD published")
n_med <- table(cmp_c$A_class_oecd_median_rule)
last <- gaps[grepl("components available", gaps$variant), ]
```

With the OECD signs (`r words(inv_oecd)` inverted), `oecd_spec()` comes
very close to the published CLI (A1): the correlation with the normalised
CLI is `r formatC(gap("(growth = \"log\")"), format = "f", digits = 5)`
(the table rounds it), `r row("A1")$matched` of the
`r row("A1")$ref_tp` turning points that `oecd_dater()` finds in the
published CLI fall on the same month, and the amplitude-adjusted index
(`aa_gap`, scaled to the OECD ratio-to-trend reference) is on average
`r f2(row("A1")$aa_gap)` points from the published one. Arithmetic growth
rates (A0), the formula written in GAA17 (p. 286, note 8), give the same
turning points but a correlation of `r f3(row("A0")$corr_lag0)` and an
index `r f2(row("A0")$aa_gap)` points away; a plain average (A4)
correlates `r f3(row("A4")$corr_lag0)`. From the data alone, cyclind
inverts `r words(inv_own)` but not `r words(missed_sign)` (A2). The cycle
of producer prices barely moves with GDP (peak cross-correlation
`r f3(pp_r)`), and the window in which the sign is read grows with the
length of the reference cycle, so that it takes in the opposite phase of
the interest rate; given as `meta$sign`, the OECD signs give back A1
(A3). The sign of a weak component should therefore come from its
economic rationale.

This first experiment starts from the component cycles the OECD
publishes, and the aggregation formula and the amplitude measure were
chosen on these same data: it checks the aggregation and presentation
steps in sample, not the whole method. Part C of the script shows where A0
and A1 differ:

```{r oecd-idn-gaps}
gaps
```

The OECD documents say that the growth rates of the components are
averaged and chained and that the CLI is rescaled "to match the
amplitudes" of the reference series (GG12 p. 9), without giving the
amplitude measure. Chained log growth with counter-cyclical components
entering as reciprocals (`oecd_aggregate(growth = "log")`) fits the
published CLI best, and the published amplitude-adjusted CLI is the
normalised CLI times `r f2(gap("OECD factor"))`, close to the ratio of
standard deviations (`r f2(gap("amplitude = \"sd\""))`; the mean absolute
deviations give `r f2(gap("amplitude = \"mad\""))`). `oecd_spec()`
therefore uses both, with `amplitude = "sd"`, and two months of TRAMO
forecasts, within the 2 to 6 months of GAA17 (p. 284). One difference
remains: the OECD published `r substr(last$variant[nrow(last)], 1, 7)`
with `r last$value[nrow(last)]` of the 7 components
(`r last$value[nrow(last) - 1]` the month before), below its own 60
percent rule, while cyclind leaves that month missing.

The second experiment runs the whole method from the original series:

```{r oecd-idn-components}
comp[, c("component", "A_class_oecd_rule", "A_class_oecd_median_rule",
         "A_median_lead", "B_corr_with_oecd_cycle", "B_tp_matched",
         "B_tp_oecd")]
```

From quarterly GDP (Denton-Cholette to months) and the original series,
`oecd_spec()` gives cycles that correlate `r f2(min(b_corr))` to
`r f2(max(b_corr))` with the OECD cycles; the GDP cycle matches
`r rs$B_tp_matched` of the `r rs$B_tp_oecd` turning points of the OECD
reference. The composite of the four (B1) correlates
`r f2(row("B1")$corr_lag0)` with the published CLI and finds
`r row("B1")$matched` of its `r row("B1")$ref_tp` turning points in the
common span; it leads GDP by `r row("B1")$ref_ccf_lag` months at the
cross-correlation peak, against `r row("A5")$ref_ccf_lag` for the OECD
cycles of the same four (A5). Classification differs most. By the median
lead alone, `r n_med[["leading"]]` of the seven OECD components are
leading and `r n_med[["coincident"]]` coincident; with the conformity
criteria of the OECD rule none passes, mainly because the dating finds
more turning points in the components than in GDP and several fail the
concordance test. The published CLI itself has `r bench$ref_extra` extra
turning points against `r bench$ref_tp_rs` of the reference, a share
above the `max_extra` of 0.4 that the conformity criteria use.
`cli_build()` then finds no leading component (B2). The OECD chose the
components with economic rationale and on an earlier sample, so the
stricter rule is a warning about the Indonesian components, not a
contradiction. `vignette("oecd-indonesia")` runs the second experiment
step by step.

## 10. A coincident index

A coincident index summarises where the cycle is now. The Conference Board
publishes one next to its leading index, and it is the natural monthly
reference when the reference series is quarterly GDP. `cci_build()`
aggregates the candidates that `cli_assess()` classified as coincident,
with the same aggregator as the leading composite, and tests the index for
timing instead of lead. Here two of the simulated series are truly
coincident.

```{r cci}
sim_c <- simulate_cycles(
  leads = c(lead_6 = 6, lead_3 = 3, coin_a = 0, coin_b = 0, lag_3 = -3),
  seed = 2026
)
meta_c <- data.frame(name = colnames(sim_c)[-1],
                     rationale = "rapid_response")
res_c <- cli_build(cli_candidates(sim_c, "reference", meta = meta_c))
cci <- cci_build(res_c)
cci
cli_quality(cci)
```

The warning is deliberate: an index of fewer than three components is
little more than the cycle of its components. The criteria mirror the
leading ones: a cross-correlation peak within `coincident_band` of lag 0,
a median lead at turning points within +/- 2 months (one quarter for
quarterly data), few missed and extra turning points and significant
concordance (`coincident_criteria()`). Granger causality is not required,
and the prediction group scores the current contraction state.

```{r cci-calibration}
cc <- calib("coincident.csv")
cc
```

```{r cci-numbers, include = FALSE}
cc4 <- cc[cc$noise_sd == min(cc$noise_sd), ]
coin_pass <- cc4$pass_rate[cc4$truth == "coincident"]
shift_pass <- cc4$pass_rate[cc4$truth %in% c("leading", "lagging")]
lead2_pass <- cc4$pass_rate[cc4$truth == "leading_2m"]
```

In the simulations the default rule passes `r pct_range(coin_pass)` of
the composites of coincident series and at most `r pct(max(shift_pass))`
of those that lead or lag by 3 months at the default noise level; a lead
of 2 months passes `r pct(max(lead2_pass))` of the time. With twice the
noise it errs more often, above all for quarterly data.

```{r cci-plot, fig.alt = "Coincident index and reference cycle"}
plot(cci)
```

`cci_as_reference()` makes the index the reference series of a new
candidate set, without the former reference and without the components of
the index, and the leading composite is then built against it:

```{r cci-reference}
cand_c <- cci_as_reference(cci)
leaders(cli_build(cand_c))
```

## 11. Graphical interface and provenance

`run_app()` opens a Shiny application (package **shiny**) that walks
through the same ten steps: data, candidate metadata, specification,
cycles, turning points, classification, composite, validation with the
scorecard, coincident index, and export. Each step unlocks the next;
re-running a step clears the results that depend on it. The coincident
index needs only the classification, so rebuilding the composite keeps it.
The export step offers the composite, the classification, the audit log,
the scorecards, the coincident index, the `CliResult` object and an R
script that reproduces the analysis. The interface is in English by
default and is also available in Indonesian.

```{r app, eval = FALSE}
run_app()                # English interface (the default)
run_app(language = "id") # Indonesian interface
```

The exported script prints `cyclind_provenance()`: the versions of
cyclind, R, **seasonal**, the X-13 binary and **RJDemetra**, and MD5
checksums of the input files and of the input data; the checksum of the
data is computed from its values, so it does not depend on the platform:

```{r provenance}
prov <- cyclind_provenance(cand)
prov[prov$item %in% c("cyclind", "md5 of data"), ]
```

## 12. Extending cyclind

A new filter is a subclass of `CycleFilter` with a method for
`extract_cycle()`:

```{r extend}
setClass("FirstDifference", contains = "CycleFilter")
setMethod("extract_cycle", "FirstDifference", function(filter, x, ...) {
  ts(c(NA, diff(as.numeric(x))), start = start(x),
     frequency = frequency(x))
})
fd <- new("FirstDifference", label = "first difference")
head(extract_cycle(fd, sim[, "lead_6"]))
```

New aggregation methods work the same way with `Aggregator` and
`aggregate_components()`, and new turning-point rules with `Dater` and
`date_turning_points()`.
